source.title: Driving the Wrong Way: Leveraging Interpretability in End2End Autonomous Driving Models

page_placements.theme: Causal dictionary-feature interventions outside text-only LLMs

record.tranche_reason: The study uses sparse autoencoders to interpret and intervene on driving-model representations, but does not test whether superposition arises from capacity pressure or whether the claim's stated geometries hold. Its intervention results report driving metrics, not those claims.
record.gate_note: The paper cites superposition and describes SAE features as sparse, interpretable directions, but does not test the superposition mechanism. Table I compares SAE architectures using reconstruction and ego-status metrics; those are not tests of the claim versions. Table II reports results after zeroing three SAE activations; these bear on the causal usefulness of the study's SAE features, not on the listed versions, so they are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The study trains SAEs on driving-model latents (GTRS, iPAD) as an interpretability tool and reports reconstruction, ego-status alignment and driving metrics. It assumes superposition and does not test any version. V4 concerns LLMs, and these are driving models. The ablation results bear on the causal usefulness of the authors' own SAE features, not on superposition.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that SAE-based concept analysis exposes how latent concepts drive trajectory scoring, including correlational rather than causal influences. They report that test-time ablation of three SAE latents raised EPDMS above the no-SAE baseline (0.5926 vs 0.524), trading ego progress for safer, more compliant trajectories. They state that understanding the concepts and their interactions remains open.
record.recipe_differences: The original source studies toy networks and superposition geometry; this paper uses post hoc SAEs in autonomous-driving models for interpretation and targeted intervention. It does not reproduce the original method.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported SAE reconstruction and ego-status metrics vary with SAE architecture, latent size, and k in Table I; the authors also describe trade-offs between latent size, feature dispersion, and memorization.

fits_no_version.finding: Jointly zero-ablating SAE latents 177, 59 and 71 in GTRS raised EPDMS from 0.4963 to 0.5926 and lowered ego progress from 0.6378 to 0.5378 (Table II).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Suppressing selected SAE latents in a driving model changes downstream driving scores, here improving compliance at a cost to progress.

fits_no_version.finding: In Table I, ego correlation for TopK SAEs peaks at 256 latents (0.8454) and declines at 1024 latents (0.8010/0.7596). Authors say ego features 'get distributed across neurons' as dictionary size grows.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Alignment of SAE latents with known variables depends on dictionary size in a driving model, so features are not size-invariant.

record.problems: The reported ablation uses a combined intervention on three selected neurons, so the individual contribution of each neuron is not separated in Table II. No uncertainty estimates are stated for these metrics.
record.rows_left_out: No rows left out from claim-relevant measured results. Table I's SAE architecture and hyperparameter comparisons are not claim-version tests; other descriptive concept analyses do not report a result testing the listed claims.

untested.parts: No toy-model geometry, sparsity transition or near-orthogonality analysis.
No test of capacity pressure causing polysemanticity.
No test of non-capacity origins of polysemanticity.
No LLMs studied; SAEs are applied to autonomous-driving models, and recovery of sparse features is assumed rather than tested against a control.

Completeness, stability and canonicity of SAE features are not tested. Authors only remark that not all neurons map to well-defined concepts, and that ego features disperse across neurons at larger dictionary sizes (Table I, qualitative).
No comparison of 1-D vs multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: No verdicts are given. The rows are correctly linked to none and correctly marked cannot_determine for this claim. Table I's dictionary-size dependence is a possible weak V5-adjacent observation, but it is in driving models, not LLMs, and is not a stability or canonicity test, so it is placed under fits_no_version. The record does not mention that the study also covers iPAD, including a qualitative input-perturbation finding about the backward-facing camera; that finding is not claim-relevant.

versions.untested_parts: Whether sparse features outnumbering dimensions are stored as overlapping, nearly orthogonal directions, and whether there is a sparsity-dependent transition or regular geometry.
Whether capacity pressure causes polysemanticity or determines which features receive dedicated dimensions versus sharing.
Whether polysemanticity arises without capacity pressure.
The claim concerns LLMs; this study analyzes autonomous-driving models, not LLMs. It does not test the stated LLM feature distribution or SAE recovery claim.

The paper notes that SAEs do not guarantee every neuron has a well-defined concept and that an exhaustive semantic dictionary is generally infeasible, but does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units.
The paper represents SAE features as directions but does not compare one-dimensional with multi-dimensional features.

relation.reason: Assumes superposition as motivation for SAE decomposition; the driving interventions do not test superposition or dictionary completeness, stability or canonicity.

tranche.reason: Uses SAEs for driving-model interpretation and intervention; reports reconstruction, feature alignment and driving performance without testing a listed claim version.

source_check.notes: The 0.4963 baseline includes the unmodified SAE; original GTRS without SAE scores 0.524. The authors' conclusion paraphrase matches the text.
